flags: Domain: every record keeps the card’s category, sermo. Many plainly belong elsewhere — natura: stick, rod, pole, twig, branch, bramble, blackberry, blueberry, bush, tree, leaf, thorn, rock, stone, ground, path, mud, puddle, cat, monkey, sea, wave; corpus: foot, arm, forearm, fist, knee, jump, hop-on-one-foot, jump-down; ludi: magnetic-tile, ball, doll, toy-bear, trampoline, play, game, chalk, paintbrush; domus-structura: wall, roof, door, window, house; domus: bed, duvet; vectura: escalator, ship, sailor, fork-in-the-road; aedificatio: build.

Likely duplicates of concepts on cards still being converted elsewhere (if the other batch uses the same headword and sense, the build refuses the second at merge): ball, doll, chalk, play (ludi entry-184, entry-186, entry-176); jump, hang, balance (ludi entry-188; jump also corpus entry-6); mud, puddle, gate (ludi entry-189); song (ludi entry-522); bramble, blackberry (natura entry-204, rubus and mōrum rubī); sea (natura entry-200); arm, foot, knee (corpus entry-69); bed, duvet (domus entry-57, entry-419); house (domus entry-86); rod, pole (domus entry-104, curtain rod and pole, narrower); roof, door, window (domus-structura entry-154, entry-157); stone, build (aedificatio entry-150, entry-153); pocket (vestitus entry-318); choose (culina entry-130); and in the other sermo batch: rest, try-again, be-afraid, ill-help-you (entry-290), grab, hold, lift-raise (entry-288), jump-down (entry-287), edge, castle (entry-245), story, tell-a-story (entry-241), wife, son, daughter (entry-312), wail (entry-313), in-the-morning (entry-517), wait (entry-281). To keep clear of other senses of the same English, these records have a sense: square (shape), draw (a picture), lift (raise), well done (praise), tear (of weeping), cry (weep), stop (cease), and the colours violet, orange, silver, dark and light.

Composed phrase terms (Pergāmus., Hīc cōnsistāmus., Tempus est dormīre., Dormī bene., Oculōs claude., Somnus mē premit., Mihi dīc quid acciderit., Tēcum sum., Hīc sum., Tē amō, Iterum temptā., Tē adjuvābō., Quid vīs?, Hoc an illud?, Ūnō pede salī., Dēsilī., Quot annōrum es?, Quō īmus?, Nōlī tangere., Nē tangās., Cavē digitōs.) are dated classical because their words and constructions are ordinary classical Latin; the card cites no author for them. Bene volāte! is ours (a modern notion). Their source line says they are composed.

Periods judged against Lewis & Short and Morgan–Owens, where the card says otherwise or nothing: artē dormīre classical (L&S s.v. artus: arte et graviter dormire, Cic. Div. 1.59), though the card cites only Traupman 313; rīsum effundere, in somnum dēlābī and Rēctē factum! marked modern, since I found no ancient instance (L&S has none; Traupman 94, 306, 101 only); Bene factum! classical (L&S s.v. bene; Ter. Hec. 456 in loci-terentius). myrtillus medieval: not in L&S, and M-O s.v. berry: blueberry: bilberry marks it + (Latham, 13th c.), where the card says “post-Classical”. vaccīnium Americānum modern (M-O s.v. berry: blueberry gives vaccīnium (Americānum)). magnēticus post-classical on the card’s word (Claudian), but L&S lacks it and M-O s.v. magnetic cites only Egger: the Claudian passage wants checking. ursulus is not in L&S although the card links it there: marked modern. mōrum rubī marked ours as the card’s “descriptive use” (L&S gives mōrum alone for the blackberry, Ov. M. 1.105). in ulnīs tenēre: L&S calls ulna “the arm” poetic (Cat. 17.13, Prop., Ov.); the card gives no register label.

Personal names: comments that named the family now say “the boy” or “the child” (bacillum, scālae quae ipsae eunt, Quō īmus?, Cūr?, the Jam advēnimus example, Cavē nē cadās, the two games, mūnus). The remark “Baba is Theo’s proavia and Raja’s avia” is not carried: the Libellus IV gloss quoted in great-grandmother says the same. The term Tē amō is the card’s “Tē amō, Theodōre.” without the vocative, which stays in the example. Libellus citations that also named a classical source (“Plaut. Persa 114; quoted in Libellus I”, “Mt 9, 5 … quoted in Libellus I”, “Plaut. Capt. 900; quoted in Libellus VI”, “Plaut. Most. 324; also in Libellus II”, “Libellus IV, gloss on Baba”) now cite the libellus formally, as check_libelli.py requires, with the classical citation moved into the English; two of them are found in a gloss, not the body (Libellus IV, Libellus II).

Recommendations kept as the card has them: stick leads with baculum, though the card says the readers use bacillum for the boy’s stick; wake up leads with ēvigilō (expergīscor alternative); orange leads with Traupman’s aurantius (modern) ahead of the classical lūteus.

Splits to check: quaerō is in two records (look-for, ask), as its gloss “seek or ask” covers both; the card’s only Latin for “rest” is in examples, so the rest record’s term is the infinitive quiēscere as printed (the lemma quiēscō is on entry-290); “stop” on entry-29 exists only as Hīc cōnsistāmus. (let’s-stop-here), and dēsinō is stop-cease; the eight spatial words of entry-32 (suprā … post) have no English on the card: their headwords above, under, next-to, between, inside, outside, in-front-of and behind are mine; subruber is in both pink (M-O) and reddish (Traupman 252), aureus in golden (Traupman) and orange (M-O, marked modern in that sense); bīmus and trīmus, printed together, are two records.

English supplied where the card had none: the translations of Plaut. Trin. 1180, Catull. 9.5 and Ter. Hec. 353 (the card has only “the son arriving, the mother waiting”); the glosses of Valē! Valēte!. macte novā virtūte, puer (Verg. Aen. 9.641) went into the evidence of Macte virtūte!, not into the examples, for want of an English.

Bene factum! and Pulchrē, bene, rēctē! are terms of well-done-praise and also its examples, cited to Libellus V and IV, where they occur, so that check_libelli.py still verifies them as it did on the card.

Card inconsistencies, copied as they are: Nimis paene māne est is “It’s far too early” in one item and “It’s almost too early” in the other (paene suggests the second); Plaut. Most. 324 is printed “Cavē nē cadās; astā.” and “Cavē nē cadās, astā.”

No source on the card for: part, edge, castle, gate, make, daughter, grandfather, grandmother, brother, sister, spouse, old-man, old-woman, up, down, this-way, that-way, why, again, and the composed phrase records; they say so. Traupman lines for entry-72 (p. 330) and entry-77 (pp. 251–252) are inline citations on the card with no source line, so they carry no “checked” claim.
